newsitem.title: GERMANY: VAT hike idea heats German debate over tax reform.
newsitem.headline: VAT hike idea heats German debate over tax reform.

text.p: A government commission rewriting Germany's tax code has already sparked sharp criticism for its interest in raising value-added taxes, even though it won't reveal its plans for another week.

After the commission's penultimate meeting on Monday, commission sources said the group might boost the VAT one percentage point to offset part of a planned 70 billion marks ($44.11 billion) in income and corporate tax cuts.
The Taxpayers' Alliance (BdS) on Tuesday blasted the idea of raising one tax to cut another, calling the proposed VAT increase "scandalous."
"With the VAT increase, once again the politicians sneak out of the responsibility for financing tax reform and budget savings," BdS president Karl Heinz Daeke said.
"The positive growth and employment effects of tax reductions would be ruined by a rise in VAT," he said.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl is banking on massive tax reform to stem profligate tax cheating and lift an economy plagued by record unemployment.
His centre-right coalition's tax committee plans to unveil its proposal on January 23, although the plan's outline has already leaked out.
Committee sources said the top tax rate would likely be cut to 39 percent from 53 percent, but short of the coalition's goal of a 35 percent top rate.
The lowest rate would sink to just under 20 percent from the current 26 percent, the sources said.
To partly offset the reductions, Bonn has already tagged 33 billion marks in tax breaks and loopholes for elimination.
A one percent VAT hike would bring in another 15 billion marks to cushion the blow to state coffers, commission sources told Reuters.
But opposition Social Democrats (SPD) joined the taxpayer group in attacking the idea.

"The coalition can say goodbye to the idea right now, it has no chance of coming about," SPD chief Oskar Lafontaine said. "The proposal to raise VAT to cut top tax rates makes no sense economically or in terms of fair distribution of wealth."
The commission was also looking at taxing pensions and life insurance payouts -- ideas also opposed by the SPD.

"We would not cooperate in raising taxes on social security recipients, pensioners, the unemployed and middle income earners -- just so that a tax present can be made to high earners," Lafontaine said.

Other leading proposals discussed within the commission would scale back deductions for commuting costs and lower the top corporate tax rate to 35 percent. German corporations pay 65 percent of undistributed profits in taxes, more than any other industrial country, according to the Institute of the German Economy (IW).

The commission would also levy the top tax rates on single people making less than 100,000 marks per year. The current 53 percent bracket kicks in for single people earning 120,000 marks or more per year.
The commission was still debating whether to apply the new tax rates in five brackets or in a linear formula that raises taxes along a mathematical curve.
